questions.q: Describe the position of peasants and zamindars in Mughal agrarian society.
answer: Agrarian society under the Mughals, known chiefly from the Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl, rested on the peasants who tilled the land and the zamindars who stood above them.

answer.text: The peasant, called the raiyat, was the backbone of rural society. There were two kinds: the khud-kashta, who were resident cultivators owning land in their own village, and the pahi-kashta, who were non-resident cultivators coming from other villages. Peasants grew both food crops and valuable cash crops, and their work was organised through the village community and its panchayat.

The zamindars were landed proprietors who enjoyed high social status. They held their own lands, called milkiyat, and, more importantly, collected land revenue from the peasants on behalf of the state, keeping a share for themselves. Many maintained armed retainers and forts.

answer: Thus peasants produced the wealth of the land, while zamindars linked them to the Mughal state.
